problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x\sqrt{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$

feedback.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-y\operatorname{tan}⁡x={y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,n=5.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{5},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-5}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-4{y}^{-5}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{4}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x$
